narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 55.6% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) of your class, far below the average of roughly the sixth decile among students who were accepted. This low ranking signaled to the model a higher risk that you would struggle with the bar exam.

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and worked in the opposite direction. At 36, your score is only slightly below the 37.2 average of accepted students, so it modestly pulled the prediction toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the negative impact of your academic ranking.

Your family income bracket (middle income) was the third most important feature. It gave a small additional push toward failure, though its influence was much weaker than the other two.

Taken together, the model concluded your overall profile indicated a greater than even chance of not passing the bar on the first try. To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic record if possible, consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score, and explore schools or programs with different admissions criteria. You may also want to speak with an admissions counselor about how to address these specific weaknesses in a future application. (248 words)
